For codes with at least one message at each blocklength on a fixed finite channel of capacity C, if the average errors tend to zero, then for every δ > 0 all sufficiently long codes have rate at most C + δ.
For a sequence of block codes with at least one message per blocklength on a fixed finite channel, vanishing average error implies that the limit superior of the rates is at most channel capacity.

For a sequence of block codes with at least one message at each length, if rates are eventually at least R > C, then errors are eventually at least 1 − C/R − (ln 2)/(nR), where C is the finite channel capacity.

If codes with at least one message per length eventually have rate at least R > C, the number (1 − C/R)/2 is positive and eventually lower-bounds their average errors on the finite channel of capacity C.
If codes with at least one message per length on a finite channel eventually have rate at least a fixed R above capacity, their average errors cannot tend to zero.
If the rates of codes with at least one message per length exceed or equal capacity plus a fixed η > 0 at infinitely many blocklengths, their average errors cannot tend to zero.
